blocks.content: PRESIDENT OF INDIA

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 52 establishes the Office of the President of India as the Head of State and First Citizen of India.
The President is elected indirectly by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies.
Impeachment of the President under Article 61 can be initiated in either House of Parliament solely on the grounds of 'violation of the Constitution'.
The President possesses Executive, Legislative, Financial, Judicial, Military, and Emergency powers.
The constitutional position and pardoning/ordinance powers of the President differ significantly from those of a State Governor.
INTRODUCTION

blocks.content: The President of India is the constitutional head of the Indian State and the highest dignitary of the country.
He represents the unity, integrity and sovereignty of India. The office of the President reflects the democratic
spirit of the Constitution, where the real power lies with the elected representatives but the dignity of the
State is maintained by a neutral head.

The President is often described as the “First Citizen of India”. Although he is the executive head, his powers are exercised according to the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
The provisions related to the President are given in Part V of the Indian Constitution (Articles 52 to 62).
ARTICLE 52 – OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT
Article 52 of the Constitution states that there shall be a President of India.
This article establishes the office of the President as a permanent constitutional authority.
The President is:

items:
• The Head of the Indian State
  • The symbol of unity and integrity
  • The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces
The Head of the Indian State
The symbol of unity and integrity
The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces

blocks.content: However, the President does not exercise absolute power. His position is similar to that of the British monarch,
where real power lies with the elected government.
ELECTION OF THE PRESIDENT
The President of India is not elected directly by the people. This system ensures that the President remains
politically neutral and above party politics.
The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of:

items:
• Elected members of Lok Sabha
  • Elected members of Rajya Sabha
  • Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States
  • Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry
Elected members of Lok Sabha
Elected members of Rajya Sabha
Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States
Elected members of Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry

blocks.content: The election is conducted by:

items:
• Proportional Representation system
  • Single Transferable Vote
  • Secret Ballot
Proportional Representation system
Single Transferable Vote
Secret Ballot

blocks.content: This system ensures fair representation of both the Union and the States.
VALUE OF VOTE IN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION
To maintain uniformity between states and the Union, a special formula is used to calculate vote value.
Value of MLA‟s vote = Population of the state ÷ (Total number of MLAs × 1000) Value of MP‟s vote = Total value of all MLAs † Total number of MPs
This system ensures equal weightage to both population and federal structure.
QUALIFICATIONS FOR PRESIDENT
A person must fulfill the following conditions to become President:

items:
• Must be a citizen of India
  • Must be at least 35 years of age
  • Must be qualified to be elected as a member of Lok Sabha
  • Must not hold any office of profit under the Government
Must be a citizen of India
Must be at least 35 years of age
Must be qualified to be elected as a member of Lok Sabha
Must not hold any office of profit under the Government

blocks.content: These conditions ensure that only a capable and neutral person becomes President.
CONDITIONS OF PRESIDENT’S OFFICE
The Constitution lays down certain conditions to ensure independence of the President:

items:
• He cannot be a member of Parliament or State Legislature
  • He cannot hold any office of profit
  • His salary and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
  • He resides in Rashtrapati Bhavan
He cannot be a member of Parliament or State Legislature
He cannot hold any office of profit
His salary and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
He resides in Rashtrapati Bhavan

blocks.content: These provisions protect the dignity and independence of the office.
TERM OF OFFICE AND OATH
The President holds office for a term of five years. He is eligible for re-election any number of times.
The oath of office is administered by the Chief Justice of India. In the oath, the President promises to:

items:
• Preserve, protect and defend the Constitution
  • Devote himself to the service of the nation
Preserve, protect and defend the Constitution
Devote himself to the service of the nation

blocks.content: IMPEACHMENT OF THE PRESIDENT
The President can be removed from office only by impeachment for violation of the Constitution. Procedure of impeachment:

items:
• Charge can be initiated in either House of Parliament
  • Must be signed by at least one-fourth of members
  • 14 days notice is required
  • Must be passed by a two-thirds majority
  • Investigated by the other House
Charge can be initiated in either House of Parliament
Must be signed by at least one-fourth of members
14 days notice is required
Must be passed by a two-thirds majority
Investigated by the other House

blocks.content: Till date, no President of India has been impeached.
POWERS OF THE PRESIDENT – OVERVIEW
The powers of the President can be classified into:

items:
• Executive Powers
  • Legislative Powers
  • Financial Powers
  • Judicial Powers
  • Military Powers
  • Emergency Powers
Executive Powers
Legislative Powers
Financial Powers
Judicial Powers
Military Powers
Emergency Powers

blocks.content: Though extensive on paper, these powers are exercised on the advice of the Council of
Ministers.

rows: Can pardon, reprieve, or commute a death sentence (Article 72)
Cannot pardon a death sentence, but can suspend, remit, or commute it
Holds national, state, and financial emergency powers (Articles 352, 356, 360)
Has no power to declare any type of emergency

blocks.content: EXECUTIVE POWERS
The executive authority of the Union is vested in the President. He appoints:

items:
• Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
  • Governors of States
  • Chief Justice and Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts
  • Attorney General, CAG, Election Commissioners
Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
Governors of States
Chief Justice and Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts
Attorney General, CAG, Election Commissioners

blocks.content: All executive actions are taken in the name of the President.
LEGISLATIVE POWERS
The President is an integral part of Parliament. He:

items:
• Summons and prorogues Parliament
  • Dissolves Lok Sabha
  • Addresses Parliament
  • Nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha
  • Gives assent to bills
Summons and prorogues Parliament
Dissolves Lok Sabha
Addresses Parliament
Nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha
Gives assent to bills

blocks.content: The President can also promulgate Ordinances under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session.
FINANCIAL POWERS
The President plays an important role in financial administration.

items:
• Money Bills are introduced only with his recommendation
  • Budget is presented in his name
  • Contingency Fund is under his control
Money Bills are introduced only with his recommendation
Budget is presented in his name
Contingency Fund is under his control

blocks.content: JUDICIAL POWERS
The President has the power to grant:

items:
• Pardon
  • Reprieve
  • Respite
  • Remission
  • Commutation
Pardon
Reprieve
Respite
Remission
Commutation

blocks.content: This power is especially important in death sentence cases.
MILITARY POWERS
The President is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. He:

items:
• Appoints Chiefs of Army, Navy and Air Force
  • Declares war and peace on advice of Council of Ministers
Appoints Chiefs of Army, Navy and Air Force
Declares war and peace on advice of Council of Ministers

blocks.content: EMERGENCY POWERS
The President can declare three types of emergencies:

items:
• National Emergency – Article 352
  • State Emergency – Article 356
  • Financial Emergency – Article 360
National Emergency – Article 352
State Emergency – Article 356
Financial Emergency – Article 360
Nominated members of Parliament do not participate in the election of the President, but they do participate in the impeachment process.
The value of an MLA's vote depends on the population of the state, while the value of an MP's vote is uniform across all MPs.
The President's ordinance-making power falls under Article 123, whereas the Governor's falls under Article 213.

blocks.content: These powers make the President the protector of the Constitution.
POSITION OF THE PRESIDENT
Though the Constitution gives wide powers to the President, in practice he acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
Supreme Court in Shamsher Singh Case clarified that:
“The President is only a constitutional head, and the real power lies with the Council of Ministers.”
PRESIDENT VS GOVERNOR
President:

items:
• Head of the Union
  • Elected
  • Exercises national powers
Head of the Union

items:

items:

  • Shamsher Singh Case – President is constitutional head

blocks.content: CONCLUSION

The President of India is the guardian of the Constitution and symbol of national unity. Though he does not exercise real executive authority, his role is extremely important in maintaining constitutional balance, democratic stability, and smooth functioning of the government.
